newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Yeltsin, Kuchma say Russia-Ukraine treaty certain.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin, Kuchma say Russia-Ukraine treaty certain.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin, who arrived in Ukraine on Friday to end years of arguing by the two Slav states over the Black Sea Fleet, said he was sure a long-delayed friendship treaty would be signed on Saturday.

"I am sure we will sign an agreement, a declaration. We will sign a string of documents which open huge possibilities for Russians and Ukrainians," Yeltsin said after arriving at Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma's residence for talks.
Kuchma seemed equally optimistic, saying: "Even if he (Yeltsin) signed nothing, this visit would have great significance.
"What we have been striving for, what we have been working for...will be completed tomorrow. And without exaggerating, I see this event as historic," he added.
The Russian leader earlier swept aside the chief of his protocol department who tried to direct him into a waiting limousine after he stepped out of his plane.
Yeltsin instead strode determinedly up to a crowd of waiting reporters to tell them he had arrived with a great feeling of excitement and hope.
At Kuchma's residence he reiterated the Kremlin's official support of Ukrainian independence, achieved in 1991 as the Soviet Union collapsed.

"The main thing is that we are equal. The main thing is that we have no claims to any Ukrainian lands. This is a single Ukraine and it must be united and indivisible. I am convinced of this. It must be this way," Yeltsin said.

Russian nationalists have urged the Kremlin to question Ukraine's right to Crimea, the Russian-populated Black Sea region handed over in a largely symbolic gesture by the Soviet leadership in 1954 from Russia to Ukraine.
Yeltsin has cancelled at least six trips to sign a friendship treaty with Kiev, largely due to disagreements over the Fleet, based at the Crimean port of Sevastopol.
But on Friday he took part of the blame for the fact that relations have been so tricky in recent years.
"Of course, probably we are also to blame. This must be put right," he said, adding: "I come with joy and hope."
